title: Electric Cars
summary: How electric cars use batteries and motors instead of gasoline, how they are charged, and what their benefits and challenges are.
poll: Everyone should drive an electric car instead of a gasoline car.

versions.title: Cars That Plug In
versions.text:
A car goes by. You can not hear it. No smoke comes out. It is an electric car!

Most cars burn gas. Gas is a fuel. This car does not use gas. It has a big battery. It is in the floor. It sends power to a motor. The motor spins the wheels. Off you go!

Is it low? Then you charge it. You plug the car in. You can do it at home at night. A fast charge takes half an hour. Lots of these cars can then go 300 km or more. That is far!

When the car slows down, the motor makes a bit of power. It goes back in.

These cars are not new. Long ago, lots of cars ran this way. But gas cars cost less. They went far. So most folks got gas cars.

This car makes no smoke. That keeps the air clean. But a battery costs a lot. It needs metals. They are dug from the ground.

Now Saudi Arabia makes these cars, too. Its own brand is Ceer.

versions.title: Cars That Plug In
versions.text:
A car drives by. You can hardly hear it. No smoke comes out of the back. It is an electric car!

Most cars burn gas. Gas is a kind of fuel. This car does not need gas. It runs on power from a big battery. The battery sits in the floor. It sends power to a motor. The motor turns the wheels.

When the battery gets low, you charge it. You plug the car in, just like a phone. Lots of people do this at home at night. You can also plug in at a stop by the road. A fast charge takes about half an hour. Many of these cars can then go 300 km or more.

When the car slows down, the motor makes a bit of power. That power goes back into the battery.

These cars are not new. More than 100 years ago, lots of cars ran on batteries. But gas cars cost less. They could go farther. So most people bought gas cars.

A car like this makes no smoke. That helps keep the air in cities clean. But the batteries cost a lot. They also need metals that are dug from the ground.

Today, Saudi Arabia makes these cars, too. It has its own brand. It is called Ceer.

versions.title: Electric Cars
versions.text:
A car glides past you on the street. There is no roar from an engine and no smoke from the back. You have just seen an electric car.

Most cars have an engine that burns fuel, such as gasoline. An electric car has no gas tank at all. Instead, it stores electricity in a large battery under its floor. The battery sends power to a motor, and the motor turns the wheels.

To fill the battery, drivers plug the car in. Many people charge at home at night. On long trips, drivers can stop at a charging station, where a fast charger can fill most of the battery in about thirty minutes. The distance a car can go on one charge is called its range. Many of these cars have a range of 300 to 500 kilometers.

When the driver slows down, the motor works in reverse and makes a little power. This energy goes back into the battery.

Electric cars are not a new idea. More than 100 years ago, many cars ran on batteries. But gasoline cars were cheaper and could travel farther, so they took over the roads.

These cars have no exhaust pipe, so they do not add smoke to city air. This helps reduce air pollution. However, the batteries cost a lot, and they need metals that must be mined.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building electric cars and has its own brand, called Ceer.

versions.title: Electric Cars: Driving Into the Future
versions.text:
A car glides silently past you on the street. There is no roar from an engine and no cloud of smoke trailing behind it. You have just seen an electric car, one of the fastest-growing types of vehicles in the world.

Most cars rely on an engine that burns fuel, such as gasoline. An electric car has no gas tank at all. Instead, it stores electricity in a large battery positioned beneath its floor. The battery delivers power to an electric motor, which turns the wheels smoothly and quietly.

To refill the battery, drivers plug the car in to recharge it. Many owners charge at home overnight. On long journeys, drivers can stop at a charging station, where a fast charger can fill most of the battery in about thirty minutes. The distance a car can travel on one charge is called its range, and many electric cars have a range of 300 to 500 kilometers.

When the driver slows down, the motor runs in reverse and generates a small amount of electricity. This energy flows back into the battery instead of being wasted.

Electric cars are not a new invention. More than 100 years ago, many cars ran on batteries. However, gasoline cars were cheaper and could travel greater distances, so they gradually took over the roads.

Because electric cars have no exhaust pipe, they do not release smoke into city air, which helps reduce air pollution. However, their batteries are expensive, and they require metals that must be mined from the ground. In addition, some of the electricity used to charge them still comes from power plants that burn fuel.

Today, Saudi Arabia is building electric cars and has launched its own brand, called Ceer.

versions.title: Electric Cars: Driving Into the Future
versions.text:
A car glides silently past you on the street. There is no roar from an engine and no cloud of smoke trailing behind it. You have just witnessed an electric car, one of the most rapidly growing categories of vehicles in the world.

Most cars rely on an internal combustion engine, which burns fuel such as gasoline inside metal cylinders. An electric car, by contrast, has no fuel tank at all. Instead, it stores energy in a large battery positioned beneath its floor, usually a lithium-ion battery similar to the one in a phone but far bigger. The battery delivers power to an electric motor that turns the wheels smoothly and quietly.

Electric motors are also remarkably efficient. A motor turns most of the battery's energy into motion, whereas a gasoline engine wastes most of the energy in its fuel as heat.

To refill the battery, drivers plug the car in to recharge it. Many owners charge at home overnight, while on long journeys drivers can stop at a charging station, where a fast charger can restore most of the battery in about thirty minutes. Many electric cars can travel 300 to 500 kilometers on one charge.

Whenever the driver slows down, a system called regenerative braking makes the motor operate in reverse, generating electricity that flows back into the battery instead of being wasted as heat.

Electric cars are not a new invention. More than 100 years ago, many cars ran on batteries; however, gasoline cars were less expensive and could travel greater distances, so they gradually dominated the roads.

Because electric cars have no exhaust pipe, they produce no emissions on the street, which helps improve air quality in crowded cities. Nevertheless, their batteries are expensive and require metals such as lithium that must be mined, and some charging electricity still comes from power plants that burn fuel. Countries also need infrastructure, such as networks of charging stations, before many people will switch.

Saudi Arabia is now manufacturing electric cars, has launched its own brand called Ceer, and aims for 30 percent of the cars in Riyadh to be electric by 2030.

versions.title: Electric Cars: Driving Into the Future
versions.text:
A vehicle glides past silently, accompanied by neither the characteristic roar of a combustion engine nor the trailing cloud of exhaust smoke, unmistakable evidence of an electric car, among the most rapidly expanding categories of vehicles currently proliferating worldwide.

Most conventional automobiles rely upon an internal combustion engine, a mechanism that burns fuel such as gasoline within metal cylinders to generate motive power. An electric car, by meaningful contrast, possesses no fuel tank whatsoever. Instead, it stores substantial electrical energy within a considerable battery positioned beneath its chassis, typically a lithium-ion battery conceptually comparable to the one powering a mobile phone yet dramatically larger in scale. This battery subsequently delivers power to an electric motor that rotates the wheels with remarkable smoothness and near silence.

Electric motors additionally demonstrate remarkable energy efficiency. Such motors convert the overwhelming majority of the battery's stored energy directly into kinetic motion, whereas a conventional gasoline engine dissipates the majority of its fuel's chemical energy as waste heat, which explains precisely why electric vehicles require comparatively minimal energy expenditure to traverse each kilometer traveled.

Replenishing the battery requires connecting the vehicle to an external power supply. Many owners conveniently charge their vehicles at home overnight, while during extended journeys, drivers can utilize dedicated charging stations, where specialized fast chargers can restore the overwhelming majority of battery capacity within approximately thirty minutes. Numerous contemporary electric vehicles can travel between 300 and 500 kilometers on a single complete charge.

Whenever a driver decelerates, a sophisticated system termed regenerative braking causes the electric motor to operate in functional reverse, generating electricity that subsequently flows back into the battery rather than being wastefully dissipated as heat energy, as occurs within conventional braking systems.

Electric vehicles are not, in fact, a recent technological innovation. More than a century ago, numerous automobiles operated using battery power; however, gasoline-powered vehicles proved considerably less expensive and capable of traveling substantially greater distances, factors that gradually allowed combustion vehicles to dominate roadways worldwide.

Because electric vehicles possess no exhaust pipe whatsoever, they generate absolutely no street-level emissions, a characteristic that significantly improves air quality within densely congested urban environments. Nevertheless, their batteries remain expensive and require metals such as lithium that must be extracted through environmentally intensive mining operations, while some electricity utilized for charging still originates from power plants burning fossil fuels. Nations additionally require dependable supporting infrastructure, particularly extensive networks of charging stations, before substantial populations will feel sufficiently confident to transition away from conventional vehicles.

Saudi Arabia is now actively manufacturing electric vehicles domestically, having established its own national automotive brand, Ceer, and intends for 30 percent of all vehicles operating within Riyadh to be electric by the year 2030.

An electric vehicle, by meaningful and fundamental contrast, possesses no fuel tank whatsoever. Instead, it stores substantial quantities of electrical energy within a considerable battery assembly positioned beneath its chassis, typically a lithium-ion battery conceptually analogous to the one powering a mobile telephone yet dramatically, almost incomparably, larger in both physical scale and energy capacity. This battery assembly subsequently delivers electrical power to an electric motor that rotates the wheels with remarkable mechanical smoothness and near-total acoustic silence.

Electric motors additionally demonstrate remarkable thermodynamic efficiency relative to their combustion counterparts. Such motors convert the overwhelming majority of the battery's stored electrical energy directly into useful kinetic motion, whereas a conventional gasoline engine dissipates the overwhelming majority of its fuel's chemical energy as entirely wasted thermal heat, which explains with considerable precision why electric vehicles require comparatively minimal energy expenditure to traverse each kilometer of distance traveled.

Replenishing the battery's electrical charge requires connecting the vehicle to an external power supply through a dedicated charging apparatus. More than a century ago, numerous early automobiles operated using battery-stored power; however, gasoline-powered vehicles proved considerably less expensive to produce and capable of traveling substantially greater distances on a single fueling, structural factors that gradually allowed combustion-powered vehicles to dominate roadways across the entire world for over a century.

options: As a list of steps for drivers to follow in order
As a description of a single driver's day
As a comparison of the cars of the past and present
As a cause and effect: why gasoline cars took over
questions.why: The paragraph gives reasons (cheaper, farther) and the result (gasoline cars took over the roads).

wrong.A: The paragraph does not give steps.
wrong.C: The paragraph mainly explains why one kind of car won, rather than comparing past and present.

MID.prompt: Explain two benefits and one challenge of electric cars. Use details from the article to support each point.
checklist: I explained two benefits and one challenge.
I used details from the article for each point.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: One benefit of electric cars is that they have no exhaust pipe, so they do not release smoke that causes pollution in the city. Another benefit is that many electric cars now have a range of 300 to 500 kilometers, so drivers can travel a long way before stopping at a charging station. However, one challenge is that the batteries are expensive and need metals that must be mined from the ground, unlike a car with a regular engine.

keyWords.definition: the process of burning something to release energy
keyWords.example: Combustion inside the stove heated the room.

keyWords.definition: a very light, soft metal used to make rechargeable batteries
keyWords.example: Engineers searched for lithium in the rocks of the mountain.

keyWords.definition: able to recover or produce again something that would otherwise be lost
keyWords.example: The train's regenerative system saves energy each time it stops.

keyWords.definition: gases or substances sent out into the air
keyWords.example: The factory installed filters to lower its emissions.

keyWords.definition: the basic systems a country needs, such as roads, power lines, and stations
keyWords.example: The new city will need infrastructure like water pipes and bridges.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Electric cars should replace all buses and trains.
Gasoline engines are more efficient than electric motors.
Electric cars offer cleaner, more efficient travel, but batteries, power sources, and infrastructure remain challenges.
Lithium is the most valuable metal on Earth.
questions.why: The article explains how electric cars work and their benefits, then discusses battery costs, mining, power plants, and charging networks.

wrong.A: The article does not discuss buses or trains.
wrong.B: The article says the opposite: electric motors are more efficient.
wrong.D: Lithium is one detail, not the main idea.

questions.stem: What happens during regenerative braking?
options: The brakes burn a small amount of fuel
The motor runs backward to recharge the battery
The battery is cooled with a stream of water
The car stops charging at the station
questions.why: The article says regenerative braking makes the motor operate in reverse, generating electricity that returns to the battery.

wrong.A: Electric cars do not burn fuel.
wrong.C: The article does not mention cooling with water.
wrong.D: Regenerative braking happens while driving, not at a station.

questions.stem: Why do electric cars need comparatively little energy to travel each kilometer?
options: They are always lighter than gasoline cars
They are only driven on flat, smooth roads
They never need to use their brakes at all
Their motors turn most of the stored energy into motion
questions.why: The article says a motor converts most of the battery's energy into motion, while a gasoline engine wastes most of its energy as heat.

wrong.A: The article does not say electric cars are always lighter.
wrong.B: The article does not mention flat roads.
wrong.C: Electric cars do brake; they even recover energy when they slow down.

questions.stem: In the article, the word infrastructure refers to —
options: systems such as charging networks
the paint, seats, and mirrors of a car
the rules people follow to drive safely
the metal used in batteries
questions.why: The article gives networks of charging stations as an example of the infrastructure countries need.

wrong.B: A car's paint and seats are not infrastructure.
wrong.C: Driving rules are laws, not infrastructure.
wrong.D: The metal in batteries is lithium.

questions.stem: Why does the author point out that some charging electricity comes from power plants that burn fuel?
options: To prove electric cars cause more pollution than gasoline cars
To show that the benefits depend on how electricity is made
To explain step by step how a lithium battery is built
To encourage readers to build their own power plants
questions.why: The detail reminds readers that cars with no street emissions may still be linked to pollution where electricity is made.

wrong.A: The article never claims electric cars pollute more.
wrong.C: The detail is about electricity, not battery construction.
wrong.D: The article does not suggest building power plants.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the statement that people need charging networks before they will feel confident to switch?
options: People already have enough charging stations everywhere
Electric cars cannot be charged at home at all
Charging stations make electric cars travel faster
Many drivers worry about running out of power far from a charger
questions.why: People would only lack confidence if they worried about finding a place to recharge on their trips.

wrong.A: If there were enough stations, this would not be a concern.
wrong.B: The article says many owners charge at home.
wrong.C: Stations recharge the battery; they do not change speed.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: It explains how electric cars work, gives their history, then weighs benefits against challenges
It tells the life story of the person who invented the electric car
It lists car prices from cheapest to most expensive
It describes a single trip from Riyadh to Jeddah
questions.why: The article moves from how the car works and charges, to history, to benefits and problems, and ends with Saudi plans.

wrong.B: No inventor's life story is told.

questions.stem: Compared with gasoline cars, what is one disadvantage of electric cars described in the article?
options: They produce more emissions on city streets
Their batteries cost a lot and need mined lithium
They waste most of their energy as heat
They are not allowed to be driven inside cities
questions.why: The article says electric car batteries are expensive and need metals like lithium that must be mined.

wrong.A: Electric cars produce no emissions on the street.
wrong.C: The article says gasoline engines waste most energy as heat.
wrong.D: The article says electric cars improve air in cities.

HIGH.prompt: Saudi Arabia aims for 30 percent of the vehicles in Riyadh to be electric by 2030. Explain what would need to happen to reach this goal, and evaluate whether it would be good for the city. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what would need to happen to reach the goal.
I evaluated the benefits and challenges with evidence from the article.
I wrote a clear conclusion that answers the question.
HIGH.modelAnswer: To reach the goal of 30 percent electric vehicles in Riyadh by 2030, the city would need far more charging infrastructure, since fast chargers can fill most of a battery in about thirty minutes but drivers need enough stations to rely on them instead of a car with a combustion engine. This shift would be good for the city because electric cars release no emissions from an exhaust pipe, which would reduce air pollution, and their regenerative braking recovers some energy to improve efficiency. However, it would also be a challenge because batteries need mined metals like lithium and remain expensive to produce. Overall, with enough investment in charging infrastructure, this goal would likely improve Riyadh's air quality even though it demands a costly transition.
